issues.title: Stu rollout helpers: search allocation/frontier design and independent recursive-search review
issues.body:
Max asked for helpers to strengthen the rollout study and said: **“Put something in GitHub for them to pick up I will spin them up.”** This is the handoff. Start by claiming **A** or **B** in a comment here with your session/alias. Two helpers can work independently; if only one is available, start with B, then A.

### Goal and current owner

Find changes to Stu's search that improve **played full-bot IMPs per unit compute** and capture more of stronger nets' gains. Also identify which extra searched decisions produce the most **subsequent trained-bot improvement per labeling/training hour**. Those are separate endpoints.

**codex-rollout owns implementation integration, the Azure experiment runs, and this workstream.** Max has authorized two existing collection boxes: azure6 and azure2. Fresh inspection confirms both are currently loop Stu collection on runtime `30e30af88ea196b8189ff39491c83cf531797868`. Isolated setup/draining is underway; do not operate/restart/reallocate these boxes independently. Other boxes retain their existing owners.

### Read first

1. [Integrated P/H/R plan in #35](https://github.com/maxschireson/Single-Dummy-Bridge/blob/docs/stu-training-efficiency-20261114/docs/stu-training-efficiency-2026-11-14.md).
2. [Runnable rollout protocol, pinned implementation](https://github.com/maxschireson/Single-Dummy-Bridge/blob/7c79acfaa138a29d140dfef3d50f9a52216a24aa/docs/stu-rollout-experiments-2026-11-14.md).
3. [Implementation PR #38](https://github.com/maxschireson/Single-Dummy-Bridge/pull/38): `scripts/stu_rollout_experiments/{engine.py,match.py,make_config.py,test_smoke.py,batch.sh}` at `7c79acfaa138a29d140dfef3d50f9a52216a24aa`.
4. [Current coordination board](https://github.com/maxschireson/Single-Dummy-Bridge/blob/box/coordination/BOARD.md), especially the allocation table and latest log.
5. [H-series harvesting work #37](https://github.com/maxschireson/Single-Dummy-Bridge/pull/37). **codex-stu-harvest already owns H02 extraction/reconstruction and H03–H05 design.** Coordinate rather than duplicating its extractor or initiating another training experiment.

### A — Dynamic allocation and learning-frontier selector

**Question:** Which future decisions deserve a fresh recursive rollout, and which deserve expensive reanalysis as training targets?

The first prototype compares flat 128; flat 32; 32 outer layouts + a maximum of four 8-layout child searches/root; and an uncertainty-gated version. Child search has two candidates, one extra search depth, own partnership only, and an eight-ply window. Its current top-two policy log-probability gap ≤ 1 is a cheap uncertainty screen, **not a validated frontier**.

Deliver:
- A concrete next selector using information available at decision time. Consider paired action uncertainty, persistent net/search disagreement, contract leverage, expected probability of changing the card, and estimated marginal search cost. Explain why each feature could help.
- A separate label-selection rule: where stronger reanalysis yields repeatable, learnable action advantages. Operationally define the competence frontier by role/phase/contract; include one/two tricks before it, broad/random controls, and a mechanism for the frontier to move.
- A small, predeclared experiment matrix separating selector quality from extra compute. Include a random-budget control, flat-search controls, practical stopping/extension rules, and board-family clustered evaluation. Avoid an open-ended parameter sweep.
- Proposed logging fields and, if useful, a dependency-light offline selector prototype under **`scripts/stu_rollout_experiments/helper_allocation/`** with meaningful checks. Start with source/protocol design if episode data is still arriving.
- Report in **`reports/stu-rollout-helper-allocation-2026-11-14.md`**, plus a short comment here with the first experiment to run and what would falsify the recommendation.

Coordinate the training-label interface with #37's owner. You own search allocation and its comparison design here, not H02 extraction or a training launch.

### B — Independent correctness and experimental-validity review

Audit the pinned prototype before we interpret its played scores. Do not assume passing smoke tests prove the design correct.

Focus:
- Child information boundary: controller versus actor/dummy, exact history/auction/void facts, and invariance to changing hidden cards outside the child's observation.
- Fresh child posterior versus accidentally reusing the enclosing root determinization; information-set-consistent child choices and seed/cache semantics.
- One-depth enforcement; global `Seats` factory restoration, exceptions, shared-state/caches, claim behavior, identity routing, and plain/pooled history paths.
- Candidate/sample fairness when the child-call budget runs out; whether the current schedule measures what its label says.
- Null/no-op behavior, score/sign handling, paired board/common-bidder conditions, failed-board accounting, actual versus nominal compute, and whether instrumentation misses child work.
- Runtime/source/model provenance, numerical mode and variant isolation. Current child replans are serialized, so timing is not a lower bound for a batched tree.

Deliver:
- Prioritized findings with reproductions, separating **invalidates the experiment**, **bias/confound to disclose**, and **later improvement**.
- Adversarial tests under **`scripts/stu_rollout_experiments/test_review_*.py`** or a separately scoped test patch, and a report **`reports/stu-rollout-helper-review-2026-11-14.md`**.
- Comment here immediately for a flaw that should pause a running arm. Otherwise provide a clear go/no-go for interpreting the screen, with limitations.

Do not edit shared `engine.py`, `match.py` or `batch.sh` in place while the coordinator runs the pinned version. Propose a patch/new commit and coordinate adoption under a new run identity.

### Local reproduction / evidence

The source work is main-based; it imports a separately pinned Stu runtime via `STU_RUNTIME`. Local runtime used for the existing checks is research `5addd826af8b10d7343df51ada528a7327d059b6`; Azure is pinned `30e30af88ea196b8189ff39491c83cf531797868`. Build DDS in your isolated runtime with `python scripts/build_dds.py`, then run:

```bash
STU_RUNTIME=/path/to/runtime OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 \
  python scripts/stu_rollout_experiments/test_smoke.py -v
```

Four new tests pass locally and on Azure. Existing local X8 suite: 34 tests, 7 native-claim-solver skips, no failures. These establish specific implementation properties, not strength. R4c model SHA256:
`e4b689c87db2f56b98221a491757dbf348ddaea066e016f06a9331fc671197f2`.

[Azure6 progress](https://github.com/maxschireson/Single-Dummy-Bridge/tree/transfer/stu-rollout-experiments-azure6-20261114) has summaries/provenance and full-episode locations. Azure2's corresponding transfer branch will be linked when launched. Published tiny screens are development data, not adoption evidence.

All evaluation seed **2026111401** families and imagined descendants remain excluded from training. Seed **131** and the squeeze suite also remain excluded. No human-table training, no model promotion, and no edits to frozen runs/episodes. Follow AGENTS.md; use a scoped main-based branch and record exact source/config/test results.

**First useful checkpoint:** a short prioritized review/design within roughly an hour of starting; do not wait for a polished long report to flag an invalidating problem. Post status and final artifacts here and cross-link #38.

issues.title: Bidding styles, variable personas (SidVariable, Gen8Variable), partnerships and identifiers
issues.body:
Max, 19:31 UTC on 14 November: two bidding style vectors (aggressive vs conservative; points vs shape), randomization, and the same disclosure/correlation rules as the card-play styles. Then at 21:14 UTC: randomize Sid's personalities; partners correlated 0.5; SidVariable as an identifier that readers use by default; partners can be asked for estimated styles; the variability and disclosure rules public; Gen 8/9 to take the capability.

**Base:** `research/rollout-loop-20261113`, not `main`, because `style.py`, `gen8_match.py`, `make_bots.py` and the bundle the play site runs live there. The play site (PR #33) runs this branch's `109a21c`.

## Bidding styles
`bridge_harness/bid_style.py`: among the calls within `exp(-near)` of the bidder's best, the style takes the highest `log p + a_eff * action`. `a_eff` = aggressive + the hand's shape lean. A random share is drawn by the bidder's own probabilities. `distribution()` and `scaled()` are for readers. Dose calibration: `scripts/bid_style_cost.py`, `reports/bid_style_cost_2026-11-14.md`. The persona defaults (`near` 6, weights ±3) cost −0.237 ± 0.031 IMP/board across a mixed population (double dummy, 12,000 deals).

## Personas, partnerships, identifiers
- `persona.py`: play and bidding styles with knowledge (0–80%), disclosure (usually 75% of knowledge) and the correlation between dimensions (drawn per partnership). `draw_partnership` correlates each latent draw 0.5 with the partner's; `seats()` gives an independent partnership a side. `public(identifier)` is what anyone may know. Identifiers: `KNOWN = ('SidVariable', 'Gen8Variable')`.
- `Gen7Player.table_styles` / `X8Player.table_styles` (`{seat: {'play': style, 'near': margin}}`), set per table. A Gen 8 seat styles among its `near_tie` cards; an 8X seat among rollout candidates within its own margin (0.05 tricks, not calibrated). A persona's random share takes one of them at random. Seats without a persona play as before (tests).
- `X8Player.meet`: a blind bot is still told a variable population's identifier (`x8.read_variable`, default on).
- `gen8_match.py`: a bot with `"persona": {"variable": true}` gets a partnership a side per board, with play styles via `table_styles` and bidding via `VariableBidder`. Records keep the personas.
- `make_bots.py` → `configs/loop-bots.json`: adds `SidVariable` (stu4c-put + persona; floors its own kind's guaranteed contracts) and `Gen8Variable` (8p-32-v41 at margin 0 + persona). No existing bot changes.

## Not done
- No reader acts on a disclosure: readers use the identifier and otherwise read every bot as unstyled.
- Gen 9 (`feature/gen9`) is not touched. Its player sits on Gen7Player, so it takes `table_styles` once its base has this code; this is posted on the board for g9.
- No job list names the new bots.
- The cost of a whole persona (bidding plus play) is not measured.

Tests: `tests/test_bid_style.py` (11), plus new cases in `tests/test_style.py` and `tests/test_x8.py`; 78 passed, 7 skipped across those and `test_gen7.py`.

- **Analysis after each board** (`sidplay/analysis.py`, its own process, no models):

  - The pooled-defender sure-trick search (`native/sure.cpp`, vendored from `2e6ed6d`), for when you had a line guaranteeing the contract and which card gave it away; as a defender, which card handed declarer a guaranteed line.
  - One-card exchanges between the hidden hands, for why a double-dummy loss happened ("It turned on the ♦Q…").
  - Exact guaranteed tricks from 10 cards; the contract question only at 11–13 cards, for your play only.
- **Sid in your seat:** Sid's own table on the deal, with its auction, play and analysis.
- **History:** older/newer navigation through your deals; **play any deal again** (marked, kept out of the totals; Sid's table reused).
- **Sign-up** suggests a username and password (both editable) and moves the browser's boards into the account.

Exchanges in the "why" are those the auction allows, with where the auction put the deciding card. R4c bids deterministically (argmax), so Sid’s calls are read as precisely as its scorer fits them.

bid_style_guide:
# Styles and personas

Bots should not all play or bid alike: a bot that has met one opponent many times reads its cards and calls better than
bridge logic allows, and that reading is counted as strength. So bots get personalities, mostly directed and a little
random. Max, 03:35 to 03:50 UTC on 14 November 2026: personalities costing "half an imp or so" should be well
represented, "with some who give up an imp even"; then, of the average over a mixed population, "Half an imp that I
suggested before was too much". The population average aimed at here is about a quarter of an IMP a board (our reading,
not his number).

| Module | What |
| --- | --- |
| `bridge_harness/style.py` | Card-play styles: `tempo`, `active`, `high`, plus a `random` share, among the cards the bot rates within its margin (`near_tie` for a search bot, `mix.near` for a rollout bot) |
| `bridge_harness/bid_style.py` | Bidding styles: `aggressive`, `shape`, plus `random`, among the calls the bidder rates within `near` (Max, 19:31 UTC on 14 November) |
| `bridge_harness/persona.py` | A bot's play and bidding styles together, its partner's knowledge of them and what its opponents are told |
| `scripts/bid_style_cost.py` | What a bidding style costs, double dummy, and whether it moves the auction the way it says |

## Bidding styles

A bidding style does not change what the bidder thinks a call is worth. Among the legal calls whose probability is at
least `exp(-near)` of the best call's (the cap), it takes the call with the highest `log p + a_eff * action`, and a
`random` share of the time draws one of them from the bidder's own probabilities (the first version drew uniformly: at
`near` 6 a 15% uniform share alone cost 0.17 IMP a board, most of a persona's budget spent on noise).

- **aggressive** (more bidding > 0, less < 0). A call's action: pass 0, double or redouble 0.5, a bid 1 plus the levels
  it goes beyond the cheapest legal bid in its strain. The weight is an exchange rate: one step of action is worth `|a|`
  nats of the bidder's log probability (with `a = 1` the style bids a level higher whenever the bidder rates that call
  at least 37% as likely as the lower one). The first version took the close call with the most (or least) action
  whatever the weight, so only the sign and `near` mattered, and a reader told half of a style read it as all of it.
- **shape** (values shape > 0, high cards < 0). It moves the aggression for this hand: a shape bidder adds
  `s * z_D` (distribution points: one a card past four in a suit, void 3, singleton 2, doubleton 1; standardised, exact
  mean 2.575 and sd 1.764 over all hands), a points bidder adds `|s| * z_H` (high-card points, mean 10, sd 4.13), each
  clipped to [-2, 2]. Across hands it averages zero: it changes which hands bid more, not how much.

`bid_style.distribution` gives the exact probability of every call under a style (what a reader needs), and
`bid_style.scaled(style, f)` the style as a reader who knows a share `f` of it models it.

Hooks: `scripts/gen8_match.py` gives a bot whose spec has `bid_style` its own `StyledBidder` (bidders are shared between
bots that use the same net) and records each styled call as behaviour `styled` with its probability under the style.
Only BEN-format nets (`predict`) can be styled; system bidders (`call`) give no probabilities. The play server
(`play/sidplay/engine.py`) does the same for a bundle whose spec has `bid_style`.

## Personas: knowledge, disclosure, correlation

Max, 04:02 to 04:10 UTC on 14 November (for play styles; at 19:31 UTC the same for bidding). Per dimension:

- **knowledge**: the share of the style the partner knows, 0 to 80% (the partner reads a styled bot with each weight
  times this share);
- **disclosure**: what the opponents are told, usually 75% of the partner's knowledge, from 0 to 150% of it (mode 0.75);
- correlated across dimensions: one correlation per persona, triangular on [-0.2, 0.8] with mode 0.6, for the latent
  normals behind the knowledge shares and behind the disclosure ratios.

`persona.draw` makes one (bidding dose: `bid_near`, a margin or a range drawn per persona, and `bid_scale`, the
bidding weights uniform on `[-bid_scale, bid_scale]`); `persona.view(persona, 'partner' | 'opponent')` gives the styles
as each should model them; `persona.disclosure_text` puts the disclosed part in words.

**Partial knowledge of a card-play style.** `style.py` keeps the best-scoring cards among the near ties, so only the
ratios between a play style's weights matter: multiplying every weight by the same share changes nothing, and a reader
who knows 30% of a one-dimension play style models all of it. For play, `view`'s scaled weights are only meaningful
across dimensions; the reading that gives a share its meaning is a mixture (the style in force with probability equal to
the share, the plain choice otherwise). That is for whoever builds the readers; `style.py` is unchanged, since the
loop's self-play uses it.

**Not built yet:** the readers. The belief nets, the hand-fit scorer and the rollouts' opponent models read every bot
as unstyled, so for now no partner uses its knowledge and no opponent its disclosure. Reading a styled bidder means
weighting the layouts a reader samples by `distribution` under the view's style against the plain bidder's choice.

## Variable personalities and identifiers

Max, 21:14 UTC on 14 November: "Update Sid to randomize personalities. Partnership personalities should be independent,
but somewhat correlated - .5 ... SidVariable can be an identifier, and when playing against variable personality bots
the system should by default use their identifier. This should balance trying to make informed inferences with
information leakage. It can ask their partner for estimated styles, and can act on the (to be publicly known) level of
variability and disclosure. We should update gen 8/9 to also uptake this personality capability."

- **Partnerships** (`persona.draw_partnership`, `persona.seats`): each latent draw of a persona is correlated 0.5 with
  the matching draw of its partner's; opposing partnerships are independent; the correlation across dimensions is drawn
  once per partnership. Each persona alone is distributed as `persona.draw` gives it.
- **Identifiers**: a variable population has one bot id (`SidVariable`, `Gen8Variable`; `persona.KNOWN`, plus a match's
  own `variable_ids`). Every other bot meets it by that id, never by its persona; a blind 8X bot is still told it
  (`x8.read_variable`, default on), since it gives away only the population. What anyone may know about the population
  is `persona.public(identifier)`. What the partner says when asked is `persona.view(p, 'opponent')`
  (`persona.describe(p, 'opponent')` in words); the partner itself reads `view(p, 'partner')`.
- **At the table**: `Gen7Player.table_styles` / `X8Player.table_styles`, `{seat: {'play': style, 'near': margin}}`, set
  per table. A Gen 8 search seat chooses among the cards within the spec's `near_tie` (0 for `Gen8Variable`: exact
  ties); an 8X seat among its rollout candidates within `near` (`persona.PLAY_NEAR_X8`, 0.05 tricks, not calibrated; the
  loop's note on `stu3-pm` puts a uniform choice within 0.05 at up to 0.09 tricks a board by the rollouts' own values,
  an overstatement). A persona's random share takes one of them at random. Seats without a persona play as before.
- **Gen 8 and 8X in matches** (`scripts/gen8_match.py`): a bot whose spec has `"persona": {"variable": true}` (optional
  dials: `bid_near`, `bid_scale`, `bid_random`, `play_random`, `play_near`) gets, on every board, an independent
  partnership on each side drawn from (seed, board, bot id): its seats' play styles through `table_styles` and its
  bidding styles through its bidder (`VariableBidder`). The record keeps them under `personas` (true styles, knowledge,
  disclosure). `configs/loop-bots.json` (from `make_bots.py`) has `SidVariable` (stu4c-put with a persona; it floors
  its own kind's guaranteed contracts) and `Gen8Variable` (8p-32-v41 at margin 0 with a persona).
- **Gen 9** (`feature/gen9`, g9's branch): its player is built on Gen7Player, so it takes `table_styles` once its base
  has `style.py`, `persona.py` and this Gen7Player; its PlayerModel is where a reader would use a disclosure.
- **Not built**: readers acting on the disclosures. Today a reader uses the identifier (its settings keyed by it, the
  `'*'` value where it has none) and nothing else of a persona.
